title: From brainwaves to robotic hands
subtitle: How I built an EEG-to-prosthetic control interface — turning raw neural signals into a graph-neural-network model that drives a robotic hand.
intro: A brain-computer interface that turns neural intent into robotic hand movement — and the data work that made it reliable enough to close the loop.
author: Caleb Liu

sections.label: The problem
sections.body: Raw EEG recordings are messy — muscle artifacts, electrical noise, and overlapping signals all mixed together. The goal was to extract the specific motor-cortex intent needed to control a robotic prosthetic hand, and to do it reliably enough to be useful outside the lab.

sections.label: The approach
sections.body: I built an AI mechanical-code bridge: a feature-extraction pipeline that isolates the relevant neural signals, feeding them into a graph neural network that maps neural intent onto robotic hand movements. The key was treating the data as the hard part — cleaning, annotating, and validating the recordings before modeling, so the network learned real intent rather than noise.

sections.label: The result
sections.body: The interface translates neural intent into robotic hand movements with enough fidelity to demonstrate closed-loop control — the hand responds to the user's intent, not just their physical motion. This is the kind of work that pairs brain-computer interfaces with assistive robotics to restore agency for people who need it.

title: Turning raw recordings into a research dataset
subtitle: The messy-to-production data work that powers reliable biotech models — cleaning, annotating, and validating neural recordings end to end.
intro: Neural recordings arrive dirty. Here's the pipeline that turns bad channels and mislabeled epochs into a consistent, reproducible dataset.
author: Caleb Liu

sections.label: The problem
sections.body: Neural recordings arrive dirty — bad channels, dropped samples, and mislabeled epochs. A model trained on that data just memorizes the noise, so the first job is never the model, it's the data.

sections.label: The approach
sections.body: I designed an end-to-end pipeline for cleaning, annotating, and feature-extracting neural recordings. Bad segments get flagged, epochs get labeled, and features get extracted — the kind of messy-to-production data work that powers reliable research models.

sections.label: The result
sections.body: The pipeline keeps drift under 5% across cohorts and hands downstream models a consistent, well-annotated dataset. Clean data turned a research curiosity into something reproducible.

title: Quantifying motor signatures across cohorts
subtitle: Turning clinical observations into a structured, reproducible dataset for downstream ML classification.
intro: A pilot study that quantifies motor-function differences between cohorts — and whether those differences are measurable enough to classify.
author: Caleb Liu

sections.label: The problem
sections.body: Motor differences between cohorts are real but hard to see by eye. The question was whether those differences were measurable and structured enough to classify.

sections.label: The approach
sections.body: I researched and quantified differences in motor-function signatures between autistic and neurotypical subjects, turning clinical observations into a structured, reproducible dataset for downstream ML classification.

sections.label: The result
sections.body: The signatures separated cleanly enough to build a classifier on top of them. It's a research tool, not a diagnostic — but it shows the signal is there.
